concepts.content: If the domestic interest rate is above the international interest rate, then the exchange rate today has to be above the expected exchange rate, because that will give an expected depreciation of the currency, which will compensate for the fact that the domestic bond is paying a higher interest rate than the international bond. Conversely, if the domestic bond is paying a lower interest rate, then the exchange rate today is very depreciated, because you have to expect it to appreciate in order to compensate for the interest rate differential.

explanations.content: A higher domestic interest rate relative to the international rate implies that the current exchange rate must be higher than the expected future exchange rate, creating an expected depreciation that offsets the higher return on domestic bonds. When the domestic interest rate is lower, the current exchange rate must be undervalued (depreciated) so that the currency is expected to appreciate, compensating for the lower return on domestic bonds.
